overview: Mendelian inheritance follows simple dominant/recessive rules; non-Mendelian inheritance covers the many patterns that don't fit that neat model.
genZNote: Mendelian: peas keeping it simple. Non-Mendelian: genetics throwing in plot twists.

aspects.label: Inheritance Pattern
aspects.valueA: Follows simple dominant-recessive segregation, producing predictable ratios (e.g. 3:1).
aspects.valueB: Includes codominance, incomplete dominance, polygenic traits, and cytoplasmic inheritance — ratios don't fit simple 3:1 patterns.

aspects.label: Number of Genes Involved
aspects.valueA: Typically one gene controlling one trait.
aspects.valueB: Often multiple genes (polygenic) or genes with more complex allele interactions.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Tallness vs dwarfism in pea plants.
aspects.valueB: Human skin colour (polygenic) or ABO blood groups (multiple alleles/codominance).

aspects.label: Chromosomal Location
aspects.valueA: Genes on nuclear chromosomes, following standard segregation.
aspects.valueB: Can include mitochondrial/cytoplasmic genes, inherited only from the mother.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: ABO blood group inheritance is a classic 'non-Mendelian' example because it involves multiple alleles and codominance.
overlay.memoryTrick: If the ratio isn't a clean 3:1 or 1:1, suspect non-Mendelian inheritance.
overlay.commonMisconception: Non-Mendelian doesn't mean Mendel was wrong — it means the trait involves mechanisms beyond his original pea-plant model.
